newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Sri Lankan hotel retains colonial-era character.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sri Lankan hotel retains colonial-era character.

text.p: Sip a sundowner on the verandah of the Galle Face Hotel and take flight in a colonial time machine.
For this Grand Old Lady of Asian hotels has all the understated elegance and faded charms of a bygone era.
Elderly waiters in crisp white uniforms pad silently up with a gin and tonic. Guests lulled by the gentle roar of the surf gaze at the sunset over the Indian Ocean.

Antiquated elevators trundle up to airy and palatial rooms stuffed with antiques. But the management would very much prefer you to use the stairs. "It is good for you. Please walk down. One flight only," says a notice.
Non-smokers get a 10 percent discount. Again guests are exhorted: "Please don't smoke in bed because the ashes we find in the morning may be yours."
A STELLAR GUEST LIST But this is no austere refuge for
the non-smoking fitness fanatic.
The hotel, built two years before Sri Lanka constructed its first railway, is truly an elegant relic that has fought a successful rearguard action against the ravages of time.
The guest list for the past 133 years reads like a Who's Who of royalty and Hollywood.
"Happiness is the Galle Face Hotel" was the simple tribute penned by the Aga Khan.
You may well be sleeping in the four-poster bed once occupied by Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh. Alec Guinness relaxed here after the rigours of filming "Bridge over the River Kwai" up country.
Japan's Emperor Hirohito, Queen Ingrid of Denmark and Britain's Prince Philip have all enjoyed the baths that are the size of small swimming pools.
CHANGE COMES SLOWLY, OR NOT AT ALL

They even joined the Friends of the Galle Face admiration society to ensure that this historical slice of the old British Raj does not disappear on this tear-shaped tropical island off the southern coast of India.
Cole Porter, Noel Coward, George Bernard Shaw -- the guest list is endless at the hotel that amiable eccentric Cyril Gardiner turned into a Sri Lankan institution.
He died last year aged 74 after suffering a heart attack on the dance floor. His suave 27-year-old son Sanjeev Gardiner has taken up the mantle with pride.
"The Galle Face Hotel is something that absorbs you. When you come back, somebody remembers you from the heart," the Melbourne-educated Sanjeev boasted.
Many of the staff have been there for 50 years. No one ever gets sacked. The service may be slow, the lights might flicker and the teak floorboards creak, but no one cares.
Gardiner loves to quote actress Carrie Fisher's reaction when she stayed at the hotel: "You could be alone here without ever feeling lonely."
After five years of negotiations, a refurbishment deal broke down with DBS Holdings of Singapore, which had redeveloped another Grand Old Lady of Asia -- Singapore's Raffles Hotel.
Gardiner, the first to admit the red carpets are fraying at the edges, said: "We will now do the improvements ourselves section by section and not be overstretched and borrow money."
A SOURCE OF LITERARY INSPIRATION

In the sweeping lobby stands an appropriate monument to this time machine. It is a bust of science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke who wrote the last chapters of "3001: The Final Odyssey" in the hotel.
"Never in my life have I worked in more comfortable surroundings, or for that matter, more inspirational ones," he wrote afterwards.
Beside the bust stand two vats of water filled with frangipani petals. Birds nesting in the rafters of the hotel lobby can swoop down to drink.
In an era when international travellers fly from one elegantly attired box to another, Gardiner says: "We do not want to be all granite, marble and chandeliers."
Ninety percent of the Galle Face Hotel's clients are repeat guests and as Gardiner scuttles off to a cocktail reception given by the Sri Lanka-U.K. Society, he feels he must be doing something right.
A couple sipping chilled beer on the verandah hold hands, sigh contentedly and settle down for the best free show in town -- the sun setting in a palette of colours over the Indian Ocean.
Time is standing still and they are loving every minute of it.
